results.name: recency_last_vs_first_example
results.description: Among multi-example trials, yes-rate when the target is numerically closer to the last-shown example minus when closer to the first-shown; the model is order-invariant, so observed above null means a recency effect (below null a primacy effect).
results.code:
# name: recency_last_vs_first_example
# description: Among multi-example trials, yes-rate when the target is numerically closer to the last-shown example minus when closer to the first-shown; the model is order-invariant, so observed above null means a recency effect (below null a primacy effect).
def _ex(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values.astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values.astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    return ex, t, r

def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, r = _ex(df)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    last = ex[np.arange(len(t)), np.maximum(n - 1, 0)]
    dl = np.abs(last - t); dfirst = np.abs(ex[:, 0] - t)
    ml = (n >= 2) & (dl < dfirst); mf = (n >= 2) & (dfirst < dl)
    if not ml.any() or not mf.any(): return 0.0
    return float(r[ml].mean() - r[mf].mean())

results.name: single_example_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on trials with a single example (excluding target == example); observed above null means humans generalise more broadly from one example than the model's size-principle posterior does.
results.code:
# name: single_example_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate on trials with a single example (excluding target == example); observed above null means humans generalise more broadly from one example than the model's size-principle posterior does.
def _ex(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values.astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values.astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    return ex, t, r

def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, r = _ex(df)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    m = (n == 1) & (ex[:, 0] != t)
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: trial_index_yes_correlation
results.description: Pearson correlation between trial_index and the yes response; the model has no time dependence, so observed away from null means yes-rate drifts across the session (positive = more yes later, negative = fewer).
results.code:
# name: trial_index_yes_correlation
# description: Pearson correlation between trial_index and the yes response; the model has no time dependence, so observed away from null means yes-rate drifts across the session (positive = more yes later, negative = fewer).
def _ex(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values.astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values.astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    return ex, t, r

def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, r = _ex(df)
    ti = df["trial_index"].astype(float).values
    if ti.std() == 0 or r.std() == 0: return 0.0
    return float(np.corrcoef(ti, r)[0, 1])

results.name: shared_last_digit_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate for non-example targets sharing their final digit with at least one example and lying more than 5 from every example; observed above null means humans use surface digit similarity more than the model's final-digit rules imply, below null less.
results.code:
# name: shared_last_digit_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate for non-example targets sharing their final digit with at least one example and lying more than 5 from every example; observed above null means humans use surface digit similarity more than the model's final-digit rules imply, below null less.
def _ex(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values.astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values.astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    return ex, t, r

def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, r = _ex(df)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    share = np.nansum(np.mod(ex, 10) == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None], axis=1) > 0
    m = share & (d > 5)
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: yes_rate_slope_on_n_examples
results.description: OLS slope of the yes response on the number of examples (1-4); observed more negative than null means humans tighten generalisation with more examples faster than the model, less negative means slower.
results.code:
# name: yes_rate_slope_on_n_examples
# description: OLS slope of the yes response on the number of examples (1-4); observed more negative than null means humans tighten generalisation with more examples faster than the model, less negative means slower.
def _ex(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values.astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values.astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    return ex, t, r

def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, r = _ex(df)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1).astype(float)
    if n.std() == 0: return 0.0
    return float(np.cov(n, r, bias=True)[0, 1] / n.var())

results.name: far_outside_range_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate for targets lying more than 10 below the smallest or above the largest example; observed above null means humans accept far out-of-range numbers more than the model (whose intervals cannot reach them) predicts.
results.code:
# name: far_outside_range_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate for targets lying more than 10 below the smallest or above the largest example; observed above null means humans accept far out-of-range numbers more than the model (whose intervals cannot reach them) predicts.
def _ex(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values.astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values.astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    return ex, t, r

def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, r = _ex(df)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    m = (t < lo - 10) | (t > hi + 10)
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: target_in_set_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on trials where the target is itself one of the examples; observed below null means humans reject shown examples more often than the model's near-certain inclusion (the model over-produces yes here).
results.code:
# name: target_in_set_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate on trials where the target is itself one of the examples; observed below null means humans reject shown examples more often than the model's near-certain inclusion (the model over-produces yes here).

    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values

def test_statistic(df):

results.name: near_nonmember_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate for targets 1-5 away from the nearest example (not equal to any example); observed above null means humans generalise to numeric neighbours more than the model's rule/interval posterior predicts, below null means less.
results.code:
# name: near_nonmember_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate for targets 1-5 away from the nearest example (not equal to any example); observed above null means humans generalise to numeric neighbours more than the model's rule/interval posterior predicts, below null means less.
def _ex(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values.astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values.astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    return ex, t, r

def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, r = _ex(df)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    m = (d >= 1) & (d <= 5)
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0
